item.description: Welcome back to Media Apocalypse, our series about the threats facing journalism, news gathering, and the flow of information on matters of public concern in our democracy, and dedicated to exploring solutions, both legal and otherwise, for preserving the press function. item.title: NYU Professor Jay Rosen Tears Chuck Todd Over Trump Lies
item.description: Jay Rosen critiques Chuck Todd's Rolling Stone interview, where Todd admits naiveté regarding Republican misinformation under the Trump administration. Rosen argues this isn't naiveté but professional malpractice, highlighting Todd's influential position and responsibility to understand political dynamics. Rosen contends Todd's failure stems from willful blindness and a lack of imagination, not a lack of knowledge.

item.title: Peabody adds six new members to board of directors
item.description: Peabody Awards has announced new members to its bicoastal board of directors. The new members, representing diverse media organizations and expertise, will provide counsel and advance Peabody's commitment to outstanding storytelling. The boards are separate from the Peabody Awards jury.

item.title: Industry leaders provide expert counsel - The Peabody Awards
item.description: Peabody Awards announced new members to its bicoastal board of directors. The new board members, representing diverse backgrounds in media and entertainment from both the East and West Coasts, will provide expert counsel and help extend Peabody's reach through new partnerships and public engagement.

item.title: Bad headline, small changes at the New York Times - PressThink
item.description: Rosen analyzes the internal tensions at the New York Times regarding its coverage of Donald Trump. Rosen, a self-described Times loyalist, highlights the growing disconnect between the paper's editorial decisions and the expectations of its core readership, particularly concerning the portrayal of Trump's racism and the handling of the 2016 election coverage. The article notes a generational divide within the Times newsroom, with younger journalists advocating for a more aggressive stance against Trump, while older journalists prefer a more traditional approach. The absence of a public editor is criticized, and Rosen questions the paper's ability to adapt to the changing media landscape and its evolving relationship with its audience.

item.title: How journalists and the public shape our democracy: From social media and 'fake news' to reporting 'just the facts'
item.description: Rosen discusses the role of journalists in a democracy, emphasizing the pursuit of truth and ethical considerations. It highlights four principles of ethical journalism: seeking truth and reporting it accurately and fairly, minimizing harm, acting independently, and being accountable and transparent. The article also addresses the distinction between news and opinion within news organizations and provides tips for identifying "fake news," including checking sources, attribution, and using fact-checking websites. Finally, it emphasizes the public's role in verifying information and combating misinformation.

item.title: Has Trump Changed the Media?
item.description: Jay Rosen discusses the press coverage of Donald Trump, grading their performance in different areas. He gives an A for investigating Trump due to parallel investigations and familiarity with corruption scandals. He gives a C for preventing Trump from setting the agenda, highlighting the press's tendency to report what the president says as news. He gives a D for innovating on the fly during what he considers a civic emergency, noting a lack of novel practices in presidential news coverage. He gives an F for reflecting on the 2016 election debacle and an incomplete grade for addressing the fact that a third of the electorate relies on Trump as their primary source of information.

item.title: Jay Rosen at IRE discussing the importance of crowdsourcing
item.description: The article discusses the importance of crowdsourcing for journalists, emphasizing that readers often possess knowledge that journalists do not. It highlights that engaging with the audience improves trust in journalism and provides a different perspective on the profession. The piece also suggests various tools for crowdsourcing, including Google Documents, Survey Monkey, blogging, email lists, Twitter, and Facebook groups, stressing that these are affordable and easily accessible.

item.title: Trump's attacks on journalists could incite violence, study warns
item.description: A report from the Committee to Protect Journalists warns that President Trump's attacks on the media mirror authoritarian regimes and could provoke violence against journalists. The report, titled “The Enemy Within: Trump’s War on the Press,” highlights Trump's repeated use of the term "fake news" and labeling some journalists as "enemies of the people," along with government attempts to control information access. The study suggests his rhetoric, which includes aggressive verbal assaults at rallies and on social media, endangers journalists and undermines the credibility of the U.S. press internationally. The report concludes by emphasizing the importance of defending the media from rhetoric that undermines its crucial role.

item.title: NYU's Jay Rosen says 2020's political journalism will be even worse than 2016's
item.description: Two years after the first Recode Media appearance (RECORD-00784/00785), Rosen returns to Peter Kafka's podcast to forecast the 2020 cycle. He argues the horse-race frame is structurally incapable of covering an anti-democratic candidate and warns that the press has not absorbed the lessons of 2016.

item.title: Radical Rethink: 2014 Journalism Ethics Conference
item.description: This transcript captures the closing session of a conference focusing on national security and the press. A non-journalist speaker, Gabe, argues that the media, while often responsible, has exhibited instances of irresponsible reporting post-9/11, citing examples from The New York Times's coverage of counterterrorism programs and NSA activities. He contends that the government holds excessive secrets, many innocuous, and that while the press plays a vital role in uncovering wrongdoing, its actions haven't always been responsible.

item.title: Creating a Space for Ad-Free Journalism with The Correspondent
item.description: This transcript discusses The Correspondent, a successful member-funded, ad-free news site from the Netherlands, and its plans to expand to English-language publishing. The discussion highlights the site's unique principles: rejecting advertising, corporate sponsors, and clickbait; focusing on in-depth reporting; and emphasizing solutions-oriented journalism. The conversation also touches upon the challenges of unbiased news coverage, particularly in the context of the Trump administration's manipulation of the press briefing room, and advocates for transparency in journalism by openly stating the journalist's perspective.

item.title: Jay Rosen pitches the English-language Correspondent on The Daily Show
item.description: The decline in trust in journalism is discussed, highlighting the closure of numerous local news outlets and the rise of alternative, less reliable information sources such as social media influencers. The article points to the role of social media in crippling journalism's business model and fostering misinformation, but also suggests that journalists share some responsibility for the current 'post-truth' environment. Jay Rosen's perspective on the issue is mentioned, emphasizing the need for further discussion, particularly given the upcoming Canadian election.

item.title: Letter to My Network: Join The Correspondent - PressThink
item.description: Jay Rosen, a prominent press critic, urges his readers to support The Correspondent, a member-funded, ad-free news site. He highlights its innovative principles, such as no ads, no clickbait, and a participatory model where members are active contributors. Rosen argues that this model offers a superior alternative to traditional journalism's reliance on advertising and its inherent biases, advocating for a more transparent, inclusive, and constructive approach to news.

item.title: Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey interviewed by NYU professor Jay Rosen; podcast, transcript | Vox
item.description: This is a transcript of an interview between Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey and Jay Rosen, a professor of journalism at NYU. The conversation covers a range of topics related to Twitter's functionality, algorithm, and perceived bias. Dorsey discusses his efforts to improve the platform, including a listening tour, and acknowledges the challenges posed by bad-faith actors and the difficulty of creating a perfectly unbiased system. Rosen's perspective as a long-time Twitter user and media scholar informs the discussion, touching upon issues of algorithmic transparency and the impact of Twitter's design on public discourse.

item.title: Center for Media at Risk Launch Symposium, Panel 4: Journalism
item.description: This transcript captures a panel discussion focusing on journalism and journalists at risk. The moderator introduces four panelists: Arzu Geybulla, a freelance writer from Azerbaijan; Parker Higgins, director of special projects at the Freedom of the Press Foundation; Jay Rosen, a journalism professor at NYU; and Sylvia Weisbord, a professor at George Washington University. Geybulla's opening remarks illustrate the state of journalism in Azerbaijan through the lens of the April 11th presidential elections, highlighting the lack of independent elections and the dynastic nature of the country's leadership.

item.title: Why Trump Is Winning and the Press Is Losing
item.description: Rosen analyzes the organized campaign to discredit the American press, spearheaded by the Republican coalition and amplified by Donald Trump. Jay Rosen details how this campaign operates on three segments of the electorate: core supporters, committed opponents, and those neither strongly supporting nor opposing Trump. The campaign's success is attributed to factors such as the rejection of independent news sources, the failure of Republican elites to push back, and the challenges posed by social media platforms. The text highlights the risks to journalism, including the erosion of trust in facts, the ineffectiveness of fact-checking, and the potential loss of institutional footing.

item.title: Journalism’s perfect storm? Confronting rising global threats from “f*ke news” to censorship, surveillance, and the killing of journalists with impunity
item.description: This panel discussion at the International Journalism Festival will address the converging threats to journalism, including the killing of journalists, imprisonment of media workers, internet shutdowns, the spread of fake news, mass surveillance, platform-driven economic challenges, declining public trust, state-sponsored harassment, and layoffs in traditional newsrooms. Experts will analyze these threats and explore collaborative solutions.

item.title: Normalizing Trump: An incredibly brief explainer - PressThink
item.description: Journalists covering Trump face a conflict: their ethical code demands reporting on his actions and words, but his incompetence, untrustworthiness, and lack of policy knowledge render much of their work absurd and painful. This leads to "normalization", where journalists downplay or reinterpret his behavior to maintain respect for the presidency and their profession.

item.title: DATELINE-SAIGON Panel: Jay Rosen on the distinctions between “journalism” and “the media
item.description: Jay Rosen discusses the distinctions between “journalism” and “the media.” Rosen explains the important distinction between journalism as a craft or calling and "the media" as an industrial complex focused on monetizing attention. He notes that while journalists often have to work for media companies, their principles can conflict with the commercial requirements of their employers. This tension, he argues, results in a "hybrid product" and that the public's perception of commercial interests overriding journalistic truths is a primary reason for declining trust in the news media.

item.title: Prospects for the American press under Trump, part two - PressThink
item.description: Rosen analyzes the crisis in American political journalism following the election of Donald Trump. Rosen argues that the existing model of political reporting is inadequate and proposes several measures to improve the situation, including uncoupling the news agenda from Trump's Twitter feed, adopting an 'outside-in' reporting pattern, increasing unpredictability in coverage, and learning from the example of David Fahrenthold's investigative reporting. Rosen emphasizes the need for journalists to think politically about their profession, broaden their audience engagement, and build trust with a more diverse public.

item.title: Winter is coming: prospects for the American press under Trump - PressThink
item.description: Rosen details a multifaceted crisis facing the American press, encompassing economic instability, declining public trust, a broken political journalism model, organized efforts to discredit mainstream media, the rise of 'verification in reverse,' and the influence of entertainment values. Rosen argues that these interconnected factors create a severe threat to the free press and its role as a check on power, exacerbated by Trump's presidency and the amplification of false narratives through social media. While acknowledging some positive signs, the overall tone is deeply pessimistic regarding the future of journalism.

item.title: Journalism: Where we went wrong and what we can do about it
item.description: This text is an announcement of a post-election panel discussion featuring experts from various media outlets and academic backgrounds. The panel will analyze shortcomings in election reporting and explore potential improvements to journalism, particularly political journalism, and new approaches to covering pivotal moments in American politics.

item.title: Newspapers shouldn't apologize for telling the truth about Donald Trump
item.description: The article discusses a Florida newspaper's apology for being too critical of Donald Trump and uses this as a springboard to explore the challenges journalists face in maintaining objectivity while covering a figure who openly disregards political norms. It highlights the tension between seeking truth and avoiding criticism, arguing that the era of doing both is over, particularly when covering figures like Trump.

item.title: Jay Rosen, Public Radio's Loyal Critic
item.description: Jay Rosen is criticized for alleging timidity and false balance in public media journalism, but his main criticism is lazy reporting. The comments were made at a live recording of "The Pub" at Mercer University’s Center for Collaborative Journalism.

item.title: Too Much Of Podcasting Is In New York
item.description: Jay Rosen is criticized for alleging timidity and false balance on the part of public media journalists, but his most cutting criticism is that of lazy reporting. He was the main attraction at a live recording of "The Pub" at Mercer University’s Center for Collaborative Journalism.

item.title: #NN08 Sketchbook. Gina Cooper, boss of Netroots Nation, isn't smooth in questioning Pelosi, but behind her the power of millions.
item.description: A short #NN08 sketchbook post notes Gina Cooper's unsmooth questioning of Nancy Pelosi while emphasizing the grassroots power behind her.
